title: What You Think v. What Students Think
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Starting from a 1909 quotation by Alice Moore Hubbard, Stuart examines the claim that what the teacher thinks matters far less than what the teacher makes the student think. He connects the idea to cognitive science, particularly Daniel Willingham's principle that memory is the residue of thought - students remember what they think about, not what is merely presented to them. He adds an important caveat: the quality of a teacher's own thinking still matters, because a teacher can only give students what the teacher actually has (the "Peter Effect"). The piece resolves into a compact job description for teaching: get students thinking often, and get them thinking well, since the quality of encoding determines the quality of retrieval.
points: Grounds a century-old teaching maxim (Hubbard, 1909) in modern cognitive science - Willingham's principle that students remember what they think about, not what is merely said to them.
Introduces the "Peter Effect" caveat: a teacher's own quality of thought sets a ceiling on what they can get students to think, so teacher thinking still matters greatly.
Reduces the whole job of teaching to a compact two-part directive: get students thinking often, and get them thinking well.
Links retrieval quality directly to encoding quality - what's stored well is what can be retrieved well - as the mechanism behind the whole argument.
quotes: Teaching is successful only as it causes people to think for themselves. What the teacher thinks matters little; what she makes the child think matters much.

Cognitive science has made clear for us that our minds remember only that which we think about. It's such an important idea that in his primer on cognitive science, Why Don't Students Like School?, Dr. Daniel Willingham dedicates a whole chapter to it.
Because, Willingham argues, they're far more likely to think about what they are watching on TV than they are to think about what you're saying.

In other words, a big part of my job as a teacher of ninth grade students is getting them thinking as often and as deeply and as meaningfully as I can about the things that we're reading and listening and speaking and writing about.
In short, what we think and how we think matters greatly. Your mind, colleague, is a big deal. You are an intellectual athlete.
Students remember what they think about, and the quality with which information is stored is the quality with which it can be retrieved.
